wine.name: Kunsági Cserszegi Fűszeres
wine.grapes: Cserszegi Fűszeres alone, a Hungarian cross of Irsai Olivér with Traminer, made in 1960 at Cserszegtomaj near Lake Balaton.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards on the quartz sand around Soltvadkert in the south of the Kunság, a soil the phylloxera louse does not thrive in.
wine.making: Made dry from the one grape and bottled young as a light wine, low in alcohol, by the house's own account. The house names no oak for it, and its sister whites of the same range, Irsai Olivér and Generosa, are made in stainless steel tanks.
wine.glass: Pale lemon, with white blossom, pear, apple and white fleshed peach on the nose; light bodied and fruit led, with medium acidity giving a touch of lemon. Despite its name, by the house's own account, it smells of fruit rather than spice.
wine.ageing: Drink it within a year or two of the vintage, while its perfume is fresh; it does not gain from keeping.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, the house suggesting about 11; no decanting; a white wine glass. By the house's own account it also makes a spritzer.

records.table: Frittmann's Kunsági Cserszegi Fűszeres is the dry aromatic white of a Soltvadkert family house on the sand of the Great Plain: light, low in alcohol and scented with pear, white peach and apple. Open it well chilled as an aperitif, in its first year or two.
records.story: The Frittmann family farmed vines and animals at Soltvadkert for generations, on the sand between the Danube and the Tisza. By the house's own account, the boys' mother kept the farm and its vineyard going after their father died, and in 1982 two brothers of the family founded the Frittmann winery beside her house. Magyar Bor, the national wine body, gives the same year. The grape of its flagship was young then: Cserszegi Fűszeres was bred in 1960 at Cserszegtomaj, near Lake Balaton, by crossing Irsai Olivér with Traminer, and by Wines of Hungary's account it received its permit for planting only in 1982. After 1989, by its own account, the house took to bottling the plain's own grapes, Cserszegi Fűszeres among them, and it dates its first Kékfrankos Rosé to 1999 and its first bottled Irsai Olivér to 2000. In 2007 the family built the Frittmann Wine House at Soltvadkert, and in 2015 the winery was named Winery of the Year in Hungary. The brothers' children have since joined the house. The Cserszegi is what the sand does well: a light, perfumed white made to be poured young and cold, from a grape whose name promises spice and whose wine gives fruit.

wine.sites: The Csábori Kétsor vineyard, among the family's vines in and around Kiskőrös, which lies on a chalky base, unusual in the sandy Kunság.

wine.glass: A light rose hue in the glass; light, airy and elegant, with fresh acidity and a delicate, fruit led nose. The house's rosés are made for lightness of touch rather than depth of colour.
wine.ageing: Its charm is youth: open it in the year or two after the harvest, before the fruit fades.

records.table: Szentpéteri's Néró Rosé is a pale, airy rosé from Kiskőrös, made from Néró, a hardy Hungarian cross bred at Eger, grown on a chalky vineyard unusual on the sand. A short time on the skins keeps its colour pale and its body light.
records.story: The Szentpéteri family has grown vines around Kiskőrös for three generations, by the house's own account, on the sand and chalky loess of the southern Kunság. The grape it is known by came from the north. Néró was bred at Eger in 1965 by crossing Eger 2, the French American hybrid Villard Blanc, with Gárdonyi Géza, and it was first officially recognised in Hungary in 1993. It ripens early and resists disease, and it is made mostly as rosé and in blends. The family took it up at Kiskőrös and made it its calling card in three forms: a pale rosé, a rosé aged in wooden barrels and a siller, the Hungarian style between rosé and red. Its Duna-Tisza közi Néró Rosé of the 2020 and 2021 vintages were each named category winner in the selection of the Wines of the Hungarian Parliament, which notes that its grapes come from the Csábori Kétsor vineyard on a chalky base. In 2021, by Wines of Hungary's account, the house's Cabernero rosé of 2020 took gold at Le Mondial du Rosé in Cannes. Néró carries American vines in its family tree, and the wine shows that a grape bred for hardiness can give a delicate rosé.

records.table: Font's Kunsági Kékfrankos Rosé is the everyday pink wine of a family cellar at Soltvadkert, made from Kékfrankos grown on the sand of the Great Plain. Fresh and juicy, with lively acidity, it is the glass for a summer lunch on the plain.
records.story: Font is a family cellar at Soltvadkert, a wine town of the southern Kunság, where the family bottles its own wines and receives visitors. By the family's account it grows the grapes of the plain: Irsai Olivér, Cserszegi Fűszeres, Kövidinka, Generosa and Ezerjó among the whites, and Kékfrankos for its rosé. The sand around the town explains the district. Magyar Bor, the national wine body, notes that the vineyards of the Great Plain were not planted only in flight from phylloxera: many vines were set there to bind shifting sand. In 2006 the Kunság was joined with Csongrád and Hajós-Baja in the Duna wine region, the name of the great plain's vineyards as a whole. The district's rosés have carried its name abroad: Wines of Hungary reported that of the five Hungarian rosés given gold at Le Mondial du Rosé in Cannes in 2021, three came from the Kunság. The family's Kékfrankos Rosé is the pink wine of its own sand, labelled with the district's protected name and sold at home. Font stands for the plain's family cellars, whose fresh rosés and aromatic whites fill the Kunság's daily glass.

records.table: Gál's Kékfrankos Rosé comes from a family estate on Csepel island in the Danube, far from the Kunság's sandy heart, where the family built its winery in 2004. Pale, fresh and light in body, it goes well with fish from the Danube.
records.story: The Gál family's vines grow on Csepel island, the long island in the Danube south of Budapest, at Szigetcsép, Szigetszentmárton and Szigetújfalu. The island lies far from the sand ridge at the core of the Kunság, yet its villages are listed among the Kunság's in the specification of the Duna protected name. By the account of the Parliament's wine pages, the founders had worked with vines and wine for decades before they built their own winery at Szigetcsép in 2004, the year Magyar Bor gives too. Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir are the estate's red grapes, made into reds and rosés beside several whites. The rosés carried the name beyond the island. In the selection of the Wines of the Hungarian Parliament the Kékfrankos Rosé of the 2019 vintage was named category winner, and the blended Rosé of 2023, of Kékfrankos, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, took silver at the Concours Mondial de Bruxelles in 2024, entered as a Kunság wine. Gál shows that the Kunság is wider than its sand: a family estate on an island in the Danube makes its rosé under the same district name.

wine.making: The method is not stated in any source read: Hungarian pezsgő may take its second fermentation in the bottle or in a sealed tank, and the sellers' sheets for this Brut do not say which. Brut means it is finished with little sugar.
wine.glass: Light and easy, loose in structure, with fine bubbles and white fleshed peach mixed with yeasty notes, in a seller's words; a fresh sparkling wine rather than a long aged one.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk young, within a year or so of release, while the bubbles and the fruit are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; never decanted; a white wine glass or a tulip.

label.means: Hungarian for sparkling wine, the word on the label.
Dry: the finished wine carries only a little sugar.
The estate's name; birtok is Hungarian for estate.

records.table: Gedeon Brut is the house sparkling wine of a family estate between Izsák and Ágasegyháza, a corner of the Kunság long tied to sparkling wine and the Arany Sárfehér grape. Light, with fine bubbles and peach, it opens a meal.
records.story: Izsák, a town of the northern Kunság, gave its name to a grape. Arany Sárfehér, of unknown origin, was long called Izsáki Sárfehér, and the place name was dropped from the variety's name in 2000. Its lean, fresh wine has long gone into sparkling wine: the specification of the protected name Izsáki Arany Sárfehér, for wine of that one grape, records that much of it is used as base wine and that producers around Izsák developed a way of making sparkling wine from it. The Gedeon estate lies on that ground, between Izsák and Ágasegyháza. By the family's own words, quoted by a grocer, its great grandparents and grandparents made wine around Izsák. In the owner's words to a business daily in 2012, the estate grows mainly grapes few others grow: Arany Sárfehér, Kövidinka, Ezerjó and Kadarka. In 2021 Magyar Bor, the national wine body, wrote of the estate in its article on the district's hidden treasures. Its Brut and an Extra Dry are the sparkling wines it sells at home, little seen abroad. Gedeon opens the door to the old sparkling country of Izsák and to the plain's forgotten grapes.

traps: Gedeon Brut is not labelled Izsáki Arany Sárfehér in any source read; that protected name is for wine of the Arany Sárfehér grape alone.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, not drier, despite its name; Gedeon makes both.

cards.front: Gedeon Birtok: between which two Kunság towns does the estate lie?
Which old grape of the plain once carried the name of Izsák, the town beside the Gedeon estate?
cards.back: Arany Sárfehér, once called Izsáki Sárfehér.

questions.q: A guest compares Gedeon Brut with Gedeon Extra Dry and asks which is the drier. What do you say?
opts: The Extra Dry, with less sugar
Both, as the terms mean the same
Neither, as both terms mean medium sweet
questions.exp: Brut carries less sugar than Extra Dry, whose name misleads: Extra Dry is the sweeter of the two terms.

questions.q: Arany Sárfehér, a grape of the Gedeon estate, lost which part of its old name in 2000?
questions.exp: The grape was long called Izsáki Sárfehér; the place name was dropped from the variety's name in 2000, leaving Arany, golden, before Sárfehér.

report: The pick is weak on its wine, as the plan feared: three searches found no source for the Brut's grapes, its method or any protected name on its label, so grapes, making and appellation say so plainly. The read together agent should rule: keep the Brut with these gaps, move the pick to a wine of the estate with a protected name, or replace the house.
The plan's sparkling wine master of the Izsák works was not confirmed in this run and is left out; so is the estate's distance from Kecskemét and its size.
Magyar Bor's article of July 2021 names a grower who first planted Sárfehér on the estate; his dates were not found, so he is not named.
The family's winemaking ancestors rest on the owner's words quoted on a grocer's page, hedged as the family's own; the 1999 plantings on one business daily of 2012, hedged as its report.

The dropping of the place name in 2000 rests on two references (Vinorandum and Wines of Hungary as summarised by search); a further claim that the grape itself was protected in 2006 was unclear and is left out.
Nobody living is named: the owner is named in the business daily and is not named here.

changed: story: Arany Sárfehér was said to be of certainly Hungarian origin; now of unknown origin, as Wines of Hungary has it.
story: the plantings since 1999 rested on one business daily; cut, and the grapes few others grow now told as the owner's words to that daily in 2012.
story: Magyar Bor's article was said to be of July 2021; now 2021, the month unconfirmed; that it names the estate confirmed on its own domain.
wine.sites: a few hundred metres from the winery, unsourced; now around the estate's cellar on the Gedeon dűlő, the address its sparkling wines carry.
open: The Brut's grapes, method and any protected name stay unsourced after one more search of mine; the record says so in its fields. The read together agent should rule on keeping the Brut with these gaps.
The business daily says the owner worked as master cellarman at the Izsák sparkling wine works; one source and a living man, left out.
